newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Greenspan sends bulls in search for shelter.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Greenspan sends bulls in search for shelter.

text.p: Gold traders were popping champagne corks this week as investors rushed back into the market after Alan Greenspan's bluntest warning yet over the lofty levels reached by U.S. stocks.
The chairman of the Federal Reserve again showed his knack for seizing Wall Street's attention as he roiled stocks by suggesting the raging bull market was foaming at the mouth.
At the same time, Greenspan unwittingly became one of the world's best gold market promoters, having given a big boost gold prices and gold mining shares.

"Greenspan may not be directly promoting gold but effectively, he has now joined the choir of gold traders, by scaring people away from the stock market," said John Geraghty at North American Equity Services, a consulting firm.
In his semiannual economic testimony to Congress, Greenspan argued that Wall Street investors may have thrown caution to the wind in bidding up prices, even though the economic outlook was good.

"Such caution seems especially warranted with regard to the sharp rise in equity prices during the past two years," he told the Senate Banking Committee on Wednesday. "These gains have obviously raised questions of sustainability."
Greenspan's words were more blunt than in December when his remarks about the irrational exuberance of financial markets also touched off a sharp decline in share prices.
This time, he warned that speculative bubbles always burst, underscoring that a collapse of the stock market could bring about economic instability.
"Greenspan unintentionally told people that gold may be a better place to be than stocks, which seem to be saturated with the hoard of cash," Geraghty said.

After years in the doghouse, gold now appears to have regained some respectability. The precious metal this week climbed $29 to $365 an ounce. On February 12, it was trading at $336.15, nearly a four-year low.

Stocks headed in the other direction. The blue-chip Dow Jones industrial average was sent skidding three days in a row. On Friday, the index closed 47.33 points lower at 6,877.74. For the week, it was off 53.88 points.
In December, the stock market had a shorter attention span as Greenspan's market warning set off a one-day decline, and stocks later rallied strongly.

"Greenspan's statements this week were more blunt and stronger," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer for First Albany Corp. "He fired a cross across the bow in December, and he fired another shot this week, but that shot was a larger missile and it came much closer to the ship."
Indeed, the latest volley may have persuaded stock market bulls to call a time out.

"The market has gotten to levels at which stocks were overvalued and that it is time for cautious and price-sensitive investors to take it easy for a while," Johnson said. "My guess is that investors will take Greenspan's advice, and if stocks go down, perhaps gold will turn into an alternative."

Greenspan has never been counted among gold's cheerleaders. In fact, the central bank chief has preached the sermon about the gold-inflation link -- the economic theory that a rising price of gold is a precursor to future inflationary pressures.

Some critics believe that the link is nonsense. Gold reflects inflation, they say, and it does not cause commodity prices to go up, just as the Dow Jones index cannot be blamed for the current surge in stocks.

Wall Street has traditionally viewed gold-mining stocks as a hedge against inflation, but in the absence of notable inflation pressures, investors are turning to the shares for another reason. They are buying the gold stocks as shelter -- a place to hide in the event the stock market bubble bursts.
As the ranks of Nervous Nellies have grown, the protection offered by gold shares against the vagaries of the high-flying market has buoyed mining issues.

"Investors are looking across the valley and they are valuing the shares of gold companies based on their future earnings and the gold reserves of individual producers," said James Turk, strategic advisor for Midas Fund, a precious metals mutual fund.
"From a long-term perspective, there are also a lot of reasons to be acccumulating gold bullion at these low levels, which are the lowest since the early 1970s when adjusted for inflation," he said.
James Dines, publisher of the Dines Letter in Belvedere, Calif., believes that "we are about to embark on a very lucrative" precious metals rally.
"The whole inflation hedge sector is up across the board -- gold, diamonds, copper," he said.

"Everyone has gone for this hook-line-and-sinker dogma that there is no inflation, and it can't go up and there's no possibility of inflation rising...and that's not what the precious metals market is saying," Dines said.
Indeed, commodity prices have been going since the start of the year.

The price of nickel, mainly used in making stainless steel, jumped this week to its highest since last May, and copper was at an 8-1/2-month high, while palladium soared to levels unseen since August 1995. Aluminum also bustled higher.
Grain prices are the highest in about four months, and coffee has soared nearly 50 percent in the first six weeks of the year.
